section: Perspectives in Education · Ch18 — Types of Curriculum (Complete)
subject: Perspectives in Education
stem: Students learn to queue in order, raise their hands before speaking, and respect punctuality — not because any textbook teaches these explicitly, but because the school environment and daily routines implicitly instill them. This unofficial, unwritten set of lessons is called the:
explanation: The hidden curriculum refers to the implicit values, behaviours and norms schools teach through their structure, routines and social environment, without ever being written into any official syllabus.

section: Perspectives in Education · Ch18 — Types of Curriculum (Complete)
subject: Perspectives in Education
stem: A school's syllabus never includes any lessons on financial literacy, mental health awareness, or environmental sustainability — these topics are simply absent, by omission rather than explicit rejection. Elliot Eisner termed such deliberately or inadvertently excluded content the:
explanation: The null curriculum is what schools do NOT teach — options and perspectives left out of the curriculum, which Eisner argued matters as much as what IS taught, since the omission itself shapes students' worldview.

section: Perspectives in Education · Ch18 — Types of Curriculum (Complete)
subject: Perspectives in Education
stem: The officially prescribed set of subjects, textbooks and syllabus content that a school board mandates for each class is called the:
explanation: The formal/explicit curriculum is the officially documented, intended content — textbooks, syllabus, and prescribed learning outcomes — distinct from the hidden curriculum (implicit values taught through school culture) or the null curriculum (content left out).

section: Perspectives in Education · Ch18 — Types of Curriculum (Complete)
subject: Perspectives in Education
stem: Sports, debate club, music classes and cultural activities — organised by the school but not part of the core, examinable academic syllabus — belong to the:
explanation: Co-curricular activities complement the formal academic curriculum, supporting holistic development (physical, artistic, social skills), while remaining organised and school-sanctioned — unlike the hidden curriculum, which is unplanned and implicit.
